title: Developer-Centric Inference Manifesto (One-pager)
content:
Executive summary:

This one-pager reframes Redwood as the inference platform built by engineers for engineers who value predictable economics, operational control, and low-latency reliability. We position Redwood not as a model shop, but as the runtime and operational layer that lets teams ship LLM features without building an inference stack from scratch.

Mission (short):
Make inference predictable, efficient, and operationally safe so engineers can focus on product outcomes — not GPUs.

Thesis (compact):
As open model innovation accelerates, the competitive frontier moves from model access to serving: how you run models determines cost, latency, reliability, and therefore product quality. The teams who win are those that control inference economics and operational behaviors, not just model checkpoints.

Why Redwood (core narrative):
- We treat inference as systems engineering: an opinionated runtime, intelligent routing, and observable controls that reduce token cost and operational toil.
- We provide a single developer surface across hosted, reserved, and private footprints so your code and runbooks remain stable as needs grow.
- We give engineers direct levers (batching, caching, quantization, routing) with measurable dollars-and-latency impact.
- We bake reliability into defaults: automatic fallbacks, regional routing, and transparent SLOs so product features stay online even when capacity shifts.

Target customers / jobs-to-be-done:
- Mid-stage startups adding LLM features who need low-friction, predictable cost and a clear upgrade path to enterprise controls.
- Platform teams standardizing inference across internal products that need consistent SLAs and observability.
- Regulated teams requiring private deployment, key management, and auditability without re-implementing serving logic.

Product pillars (how we deliver the narrative):
1) Developer-first API: predictable surface area (text, chat, embeddings) with streaming, tools/function-calls, and SDKs that integrate into modern stacks.
2) Serving runtime that optimizes for throughput and latency: sequence-aware kernels, KV prefix caching, and continuous batching.
3) Deployment parity: same API, rollout controls, and tracing across hosted/dedicated/private.
4) Economics and observability: token-level cost breakdowns, per-route latency, and suggestions to reduce unit cost (quantization, batch sizes, cache rules).

Differentiators (short, concrete):
- Levers > models: we emphasize operational levers engineers can adjust to trade cost vs quality in production.
- Deployment parity: no surprises when moving from POC to reserved capacity or a private install.
- Predictable failure modes: designed fallbacks keep features responsive when capacity is constrained.
- Actionable observability: token & route-level telemetry plus cost-saving recommendations that are directly actionable by engineers.

Proof points / examples (talking points for sales):
- Typical customer reduces per-token spend 20–40% in production by enabling prefix caching + recommended batching profiles.
- Dedicated customers see 2–3x throughput improvement vs naive single-tenant endpoints through tuned kernels and batching.
- One regulated customer moved from manual on-prem inference to Redwood Private with automated rollouts and reduced operational incidents by 60%. (internal case study available)

Elevator pitches (3 variants):
- Developer pitch (30s): "Redwood is the inference runtime you plug into — same API whether you prototype on our hosted API or run in your VPC. We give you deterministic latency, transparent costs, and direct knobs to tune production behavior so your engineering team ships faster and spends less."
- Platform/Infra pitch (30s): "Redwood provides a single serving stack with predictable economics and operational controls across hosted/dedicated/private deployments — ideal for platform teams standardizing inference across products."
- Executive pitch (15s): "Redwood makes LLM-powered features predictable and affordable at scale by shifting the advantage from owning models to owning the way models are served."

Website headline + subhead (test variants):
- Headline A: "Inference that behaves like infrastructure"
  Subhead A: "Deterministic latency, transparent economics, and production controls for building reliable LLM features."
- Headline B: "Ship LLM features — not inference ops"
  Subhead B: "A single API and operational plane across hosted, reserved, and private deployments."

Top objections and suggested responses:
- Objection: "We can host models ourselves; why pay for Redwood?"
  Response: "If you value predictable latency, lower unit cost, and faster time-to-market, Redwood reduces ops burden and often lowers total cost by 20–40% through batching, caching, and optimized kernels — and gives you the compliance options without rebuilding the stack."
- Objection: "We need full control over models and inference code."
  Response: "Redwood Private installs into your environment and provides a control plane that leaves model artifacts and keys under your control, while giving you the operational primitives and telemetry engineers need."
- Objection: "We only care about model quality — not serving."
  Response: "Model quality matters, but at scale serving choices determine user experience and unit economics. Redwood helps you preserve quality while making serving predictable and efficient."

Sales/demo hooks (what to show in a 30–45m demo):
1) Quick onboarding: 5–10 minute hosted API usage and SDK example calling a chat flow.
2) Observability: live token/cost breakdown on a sample route and a before/after simulation when enabling caching + batching.
3) Rollouts: demo canary/A-B and automatic fallback to cheaper model variant during simulated contention.
4) Private preview: architecture diagram showing VPC install, KMS/HSM integration, and audit log streaming.

30/60/90 GTM sprint (practical next steps):
- 30 days: create single-slide deal checklist for AE, update sales playbook with two new demo scripts (developer + platform). Publish a short comparison matrix vs three competitors.
- 60 days: enable a set of customer-facing one-pagers for each buyer persona (developer, infra/platform, security) and run 2 internal enablement sessions.
- 90 days: collect 3 public case studies, finalize a quantitative cost-savings teardown for the website, and publish an updated landing hero that incorporates the winning headline/subhead variant.

Appendix: tone & language guidance (for writers and product marketing)
- Use system-engineering vocabulary rather than marketing fluff: latency SLOs, batching, KV cache, cost per 1M tokens.
- Lead with developer outcomes: ship time, operational burden, predictable budgets.
- Avoid framing as a model marketplace; focus on serving and operational control.

Document notes: this brief is intentionally tactical for sales and product marketing drafts. It should inform the next round of website copy, one-pagers for SDR/AEs, and the demo script. For supporting material, see linked artifacts above and reach out to Jordan Lee for technical validation of the proof points.
